{{Short description|Universal hash family used for message authentication in cryptography}}

'''Poly1305''' is a [[Universal hashing|universal hash family]] designed by [[Daniel J. Bernstein]] in 2002 for use in [[cryptography]].<ref name="aumasson2018seriouscrypto">{{cite book
|author-last=Aumasson
|author-first=Jean-Philippe
|title=Serious Cryptography: A Practical Introduction to Modern Encryption
|publisher=No Starch Press
|year=2018
|isbn=978-1-59327-826-7
|chapter=Chapter 7: Keyed Hashing
|pages=136–138
}}</ref><ref name="djb2005poly1305">{{cite conference
|last=Bernstein
|first=Daniel J.
|author-link=Daniel J. Bernstein
|title=The Poly1305-AES message-authentication code
|book-title=Fast Software Encryption: 12th international workshop
|conference=FSE 2005
|editor-last1=Gilbert
|editor-first1=Henri
|editor-last2=Handschuh
|editor-first2=Helena
|location=Paris, France
|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science
|issue=3557
|publisher=Springer
|date=2005-03-29
|isbn=3-540-26541-4
|url=https://cr.yp.to/papers.html#poly1305
|access-date=2022-10-14
|doi=10.1007/11502760_3
|doi-access=free
}}</ref>

As with any universal hash family, Poly1305 can be used as a one-time [[message authentication code]] to authenticate a single message using a secret key shared between sender and recipient,<ref name="djb2001forgery">{{cite book
|author-last=Bernstein
|author-first=Daniel J.
|author-link=Daniel J. Bernstein
|chapter=Protecting communications against forgery
|title=Algorithmic number theory: lattices, number fields, curves and cryptography
|series=Mathematical Sciences Research Institute Publications
|volume=44
|editor-last1=Buhler
|editor-first1=Joe
|editor-last2=Stevenhagen
|editor-first2=Peter
|publisher=Cambridge University Press
|isbn=978-0521808545
|pages=535–549
|url=https://cr.yp.to/papers.html#forgery
|date=2008-05-01
|access-date=2022-10-14
}}</ref>
similar to the way that a [[one-time pad]] can be used to conceal the content of a single message using a secret key shared between sender and recipient.

Originally Poly1305 was proposed as part of Poly1305-AES,<ref name="djb2005poly1305"/> a Carter&ndash;Wegman authenticator<ref name="carter-wegman1981hashautheq">{{cite journal
|author-last1=Wegman
|author-first1=Mark N.
|author-last2=Carter
|author-first2=J. Lawrence
|title=New Hash Functions and Their Use in Authentication and Set Equality
|journal=Journal of Computer and System Sciences
|year=1981
|volume=22
|issue=3
|pages=265–279
|doi=10.1016/0022-0000(81)90033-7
|doi-access=
|bibcode=1981JCoSS..22..265W
}}</ref><ref name="boneh-shoup-course">{{cite book
|author-last1=Boneh
|author-first1=Dan
|author-link1=Dan Boneh
|author-last2=Shoup
|author-first2=Victor
|author-link2=Victor Shoup
|title=A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography
|edition=Version 0.5
|date=January 2020
|at=§7.4 The Carter-Wegman MAC, pp. 262&ndash;269
|url=https://crypto.stanford.edu/~dabo/cryptobook/BonehShoup_0_5.pdf#page=276
|access-date=2022-10-14
}}</ref><ref name="aumasson2018seriouscrypto"/>
that combines the Poly1305 hash with [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES-128]] to authenticate many messages using a single short key and distinct message numbers.
Poly1305 was later applied with a single-use key generated for each message using [[XSalsa20]] in the [[NaCl (software)|NaCl]] crypto_secretbox_xsalsa20poly1305 authenticated cipher,<ref name="djb2009naclcrypto">{{cite tech report
|author-last=Bernstein
|author-first=Daniel J.
|title=Cryptography in NaCl
|number=Document ID: 1ae6a0ecef3073622426b3ee56260d34
|date=2009-03-10
|url=https://cr.yp.to/papers.html#naclcrypto
}}</ref>
and then using [[ChaCha (cipher)|ChaCha]] in the [[ChaCha20-Poly1305]] authenticated cipher<ref name="rfc7539">{{cite ietf
|author-last1=Nir
|author-first1=Y.
|author-last2=Langley
|author-first2=A.
|title=ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF Protocols
|date=May 2015
|rfc=7539
}}</ref><ref name="rfc8439">{{cite ietf
|author-last1=Nir
|author-first1=Y.
|author-last2=Langley
|author-first2=A.
|title=ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF Protocols
|date=June 2018
|rfc=8439
}}</ref><ref name="aumasson2018seriouscrypto"/>
deployed in [[Transport Layer Security|TLS]] on the internet.<ref name="rfc7905">{{cite ietf
|author-last1=Langley
|author-first1=A.
|author-last2=Chang
|author-first2=W.
|author-last3=Mavrogiannopoulos
|author-first3=N.
|author-last4=Strombergson
|author-first4=J.
|author-last5=Josefsson
|author-first5=S.
|title=ChaCha20-Poly1305 Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
|date=June 2016
|rfc=7905
}}</ref>

==Description==
===Definition of Poly1305===
Poly1305 takes a 16-byte secret key <math>r</math> and an <math>L</math>-byte message <math>m</math> and returns a 16-byte hash <math>\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m)</math>.
To do this, Poly1305:<ref name="djb2005poly1305"/><ref name="aumasson2018seriouscrypto"/>

# Interprets <math>r</math> as a [[Endianness|little-endian]] 16-byte integer.
# Breaks the message <math>m = (m[0], m[1], m[2], \dotsc, m[L - 1])</math> into consecutive 16-byte chunks.
# Interprets the 16-byte chunks as 17-byte little-endian integers by appending a 1 byte to every 16-byte chunk, to be used as coefficients of a polynomial.
# Evaluates the polynomial at the point <math>r</math> modulo the prime <math>2^{130} - 5</math>.
# Reduces the result modulo <math>2^{128}</math> encoded in little-endian return a 16-byte hash.

The coefficients <math>c_i</math> of the polynomial <math>c_1 r^q + c_2 r^{q - 1} + \cdots + c_q r</math>, where <math>q = \lceil L/16\rceil</math>, are:

<math display="block">
  c_i = m[16i - 16] + 2^8 m[16i - 15] + 2^{16} m[16i - 14] + \cdots + 2^{120} m[16i - 1] + 2^{128},
</math>

with the exception that, if <math>L \not\equiv 0 \pmod{16}</math>, then:

<math display="block">
  c_q = m[16q - 16] + 2^8 m[16q - 15] + \cdots + 2^{8(L \bmod 16) - 8} m[L - 1] + 2^{8 (L \bmod 16)}.
</math>

The secret key <math>r = (r[0], r[1], r[2], \dotsc, r[15])</math> is restricted to have the bytes <math>r[3], r[7], r[11], r[15] \in \{0,1,2,\dotsc,15\}</math>, ''i.e.'', to have their top four bits clear; and to have the bytes <math>r[4], r[8], r[12] \in \{0,4,8,\dotsc,252\}</math>, ''i.e.'', to have their bottom two bits clear.
Thus there are <math>2^{106}</math> distinct possible values of <math>r</math>.

===Use as a one-time authenticator===

If <math>s</math> is a secret 16-byte string interpreted as a little-endian integer, then

<math display="block">
  a := \bigl(\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m) + s\bigr) \bmod 2^{128}
</math>

is called the '''authenticator''' for the message <math>m</math>.
If a sender and recipient share the 32-byte secret key <math>(r, s)</math> in advance, chosen uniformly at random, then the sender can transmit an authenticated message <math>(a, m)</math>.
When the recipient receives an ''alleged'' authenticated message <math>(a', m')</math> (which may have been modified in transmit by an adversary), they can verify its authenticity by testing whether

<math display="block">
  a' \mathrel{\stackrel?=} \bigl(\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m') + s\bigr) \bmod 2^{128}.
</math>
Without knowledge of <math>(r, s)</math>, the adversary has probability <math>8\lceil L/16\rceil/2^{106}</math> of finding any <math>(a', m') \ne (a, m)</math> that will pass verification.

However, the same key <math>(r, s)</math> must not be reused for two messages.
If the adversary learns

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
  a_1 &= \bigl(\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m_1) + s\bigr) \bmod 2^{128}, \\
  a_2 &= \bigl(\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m_2) + s\bigr) \bmod 2^{128},
\end{align}
</math>

for <math>m_1 \ne m_2</math>, they can subtract

<math display="block">
  a_1 - a_2 \equiv \operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m_1) - \operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m_2) \pmod{2^{128}}
</math>

and find a root of the resulting polynomial to recover a small list of candidates for the secret evaluation point <math>r</math>, and from that the secret pad <math>s</math>.
The adversary can then use this to forge additional messages with high probability.

===Use in Poly1305-AES as a Carter–Wegman authenticator===

The original Poly1305-AES proposal<ref name="djb2005poly1305"/> uses the Carter–Wegman structure<ref name="carter-wegman1981hashautheq"/><ref name="boneh-shoup-course"/> to authenticate many messages by taking <math>a_i := H_r(m_i) + p_i</math> to be the authenticator on the {{math|''i''}}th message <math>m_i</math>, where <math>H_r</math> is a universal hash family and <math>p_i</math> is an independent uniform random hash value that serves as a one-time pad to conceal it.
Poly1305-AES uses [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES-128]] to generate <math>p_i := \operatorname{AES}_k(i)</math>, where <math>i</math> is encoded as a 16-byte little-endian integer.

Specifically, a Poly1305-AES key is a 32-byte pair <math>(r, k)</math> of a 16-byte evaluation point <math>r</math>, as above, and a 16-byte AES key <math>k</math>.
The Poly1305-AES authenticator on a message <math>m_i</math> is

<math display="block">
  a_i := \bigl(\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m_i) + \operatorname{AES}_k(i)\bigr) \bmod 2^{128},
</math>

where 16-byte strings and integers are identified by little-endian encoding.
Note that <math>r</math> is reused between messages.

Without knowledge of <math>(r, k)</math>, the adversary has low probability of forging any authenticated messages that the recipient will accept as genuine.
Suppose the adversary sees <math>C</math> authenticated messages and attempts <math>D</math> forgeries, and can [[Pseudorandom permutation|distinguish <math>\operatorname{AES}_k</math> from a uniform random permutation]] with advantage at most <math>\delta</math>.
(Unless AES is broken, <math>\delta</math> is very small.)
The adversary's chance of success at a single forgery is at most:

<math display="block">
  \delta + \frac{(1 - C/2^{128})^{-(C + 1)/2} \cdot 8 D \lceil L/16\rceil}{2^{106}}.
</math>

The message number <math>i</math> must never be repeated with the same key <math>(r, k)</math>.
If it is, the adversary can recover a small list of candidates for <math>r</math> and <math>\operatorname{AES}_k(i)</math>, as with the one-time authenticator, and use that to forge messages.

===Use in NaCl and ChaCha20-Poly1305===

The [[NaCl (software)|NaCl]] <code>crypto_secretbox_xsalsa20poly1305</code> [[Authenticated encryption|authenticated cipher]] uses a message number <math>i</math> with the [[XSalsa20]] stream cipher to generate a per-message [[key stream]], the first 32 bytes of which are taken as a one-time Poly1305 key <math>(r_i, s_i)</math> and the rest of which is used for encrypting the message.
It then uses Poly1305 as a one-time authenticator for the ciphertext of the message.<ref name="djb2009naclcrypto"/>

[[ChaCha20-Poly1305]] uses the first 32 bytes of the [[ChaCha (cipher)|ChaCha]] stream cipher output to generate a one-time Poly1305 key, discards the next 32 bytes, and uses the rest to encrypt the message.<ref name="rfc8439"/>
XChaCha20-Poly1305 using XChaCha instead of ChaCha or XSalsa20 has also been described.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arciszewski |first1=Scott |title=XChaCha: eXtended-nonce ChaCha and AEAD_XChaCha20_Poly1305 (Expired Internet-Draft)|url=https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-irtf-cfrg-xchacha-03 |newspaper=Ietf Datatracker |date=10 January 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

==Security==
The security of Poly1305 and its derivatives against forgery follows from its '''bounded difference probability''' as a [[Universal hashing|universal hash family]]:
If <math>m_1</math> and <math>m_2</math> are messages of up to <math>L</math> bytes each, and <math>d</math> is any 16-byte string interpreted as a little-endian integer, then

<math display="block">
  \Pr[\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m_1) - \operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m_2) \equiv d \pmod{2^{128}}]
  \leq \frac{8\lceil L/16\rceil}{2^{106}},
</math>

where <math>r</math> is a uniform random Poly1305 key.<ref name="djb2005poly1305"/>{{rp|at=Theorem 3.3, p. 8}}

This property is sometimes called '''<math>\epsilon</math>-almost-Δ-universality''' over <math>\mathbb Z/2^{128}\mathbb Z</math>, or '''<math>\epsilon</math>-AΔU''',<ref name="halevi-krawczyk1997mmh">{{cite conference
|author-last1=Halevi
|author-first1=Shai
|author-link1=Shai Halevi
|author-last2=Krawczyk
|author-first2=Hugo
|author-link2=Hugo Krawczyk
|title=MMH: Software Message Authentication in the Gbit/Second Rates
|editor-last=Biham
|editor-first=Eli
|editor-link=Eli Biham
|book-title=Fast Software Encryption
|conference=FSE 1997
|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science
|issue=1267
|publisher=Springer
|doi=10.1007/BFb0052345
|doi-access=free
|isbn=978-3-540-63247-4
}}</ref>
where <math>\epsilon = 8\lceil L/16\rceil/2^{106}</math> in this case.

===Of one-time authenticator===

With a one-time authenticator <math>a = \bigl(\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m) + s\bigr) \bmod 2^{128}</math>, the adversary's success probability for any forgery attempt <math>(a', m')</math> on a message <math>m'</math> of up to <math>L</math> bytes is:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
  \Pr[&a' = \operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m') + s
    \mathrel\mid a = \operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m) + s] \\
  &= \Pr[a' = \operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m') + a - \operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m)] \\
  &= \Pr[\operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m') - \operatorname{Poly1305}_r(m) = a' - a] \\
  &\leq 8\lceil L/16\rceil/2^{106}.
\end{align}
</math>

Here arithmetic inside the <math>\Pr[\cdots]</math> is taken to be in <math>\mathbb Z/2^{128}\mathbb Z</math> for simplicity.

===Of NaCl and ChaCha20-Poly1305===

For [[NaCl (software)|NaCl]] crypto_secretbox_xsalsa20poly1305 and [[ChaCha20-Poly1305]], the adversary's success probability at forgery is the same for each message independently as for a one-time authenticator, plus the adversary's distinguishing advantage <math>\delta</math> against XSalsa20 or ChaCha as [[Pseudorandom function|pseudorandom functions]] used to generate the per-message key.
In other words, the probability that the adversary succeeds at a single forgery after <math>D</math> attempts of messages up to <math>L</math> bytes is at most:

<math display="block">
  \delta + \frac{8D \lceil L/16\rceil}{2^{106}}.
</math>

===Of Poly1305-AES===

The security of Poly1305-AES against forgery follows from the Carter&ndash;Wegman&ndash;Shoup structure, which instantiates a Carter&ndash;Wegman authenticator with a permutation to generate the per-message pad.<ref name="djb2005securitywcs">{{cite conference
|author-last=Bernstein
|author-first=Daniel J.
|author-link=Daniel J. Bernstein
|title=Stronger security bounds for Wegman-Carter-Shoup authenticators
|book-title=Advances in Cryptology&mdash;EUROCRYPT 2005, 24th annual international conference on the theory and applications of cryptographic techniques
|conference=EUROCRYPT 2005
|editor-last=Cramer
|editor-first=Ronald
|location=Aarhus, Denmark
|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science
|issue=3494
|publisher=Springer
|isbn=3-540-25910-4
|date=2005-02-27
|url=https://cr.yp.to/papers.html#securitywcs
|doi=10.1007/11426639_10
|doi-access=free
}}</ref>
If an adversary sees <math>C</math> authenticated messages and attempts <math>D</math> forgeries of messages of up to <math>L</math> bytes, and if the adversary has distinguishing advantage at most <math>\delta</math> against AES-128 as a [[pseudorandom permutation]], then the probability the adversary succeeds at any one of the <math>D</math> forgeries is at most:<ref name="djb2005poly1305"/>

<math display="block">
  \delta + \frac{(1 - C/2^{128})^{-(C + 1)/2} \cdot 8 D \lceil L/16\rceil}{2^{106}}.
</math>

{{quote|For instance, assuming that messages are packets up to 1024 bytes; that the attacker sees 2<sup>64</sup> messages authenticated under a Poly1305-AES key; that the attacker attempts a whopping 2<sup>75</sup> forgeries; and that the attacker cannot break AES with probability above δ; then, with probability at least 0.999999 − δ, all the 2<sup>75</sup> are rejected|Bernstein, Daniel J. (2005)<ref name="djb2005poly1305"/>}}

==Speed==
Poly1305-AES can be computed at high speed in various CPUs: for an ''n''-byte message, no more than 3.1''n'' + 780 Athlon cycles are needed,<ref name="djb2005poly1305"/> for example.
The author has released optimized [[source code]] for [[Athlon]], [[Pentium]] Pro/II/III/M, [[PowerPC]], and [[UltraSPARC]], in addition to non-optimized [[reference implementation]]s in [[C (programming language)|C]] and [[C++]] as [[public domain software]].<ref>[https://cr.yp.to/mac.html A state-of-the-art message-authentication code] on cr.yp.to</ref>
